newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls McVeigh verdict "long overdue day".
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls McVeigh verdict "long overdue day".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday said Timothy McVeigh's guilty verdict in the Oklahoma City bombing marked a "long overdue day" for the survivors of the people killed in the blast.

Clinton, whose own security was increased as a result of the bombing, declined comment on a Denver jury's finding of McVeigh guilty on all counts in the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995.
"But I will say that this is a very important and long overdue day for the survivors and families of those who died in Oklahoma City," he said.

Clinton was constrained from commenting because the jury must now decide McVeigh's sentence and a second defendant in the bombing, Terry Nichols, is to stand trial. He wanted to do nothing to prejudice the legal process.

Clinton, who in the immediate wake of the bombing had pledged that justice would be "swift, certain and severe," said he was particularly proud of the work done by Attorney General Janet Reno, the prosecutors, the FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms.

"Two years ago, I spoke to the families of the 168 people who lost their lives at the Murrah federal building," Clinton said. "I told them that though they had lost much, they had not lost everything -- and they had not lost America.

"I pledged then and I pledge now that we will stand with them for as many tomorrows as it takes. Today, I say to the families of the victims, no single verdict can bring an end to your anguish. But your courage has been an inspiration to all Americans. Our prayers are with you," he said.
Justice Department officials said the verdict brought "a sense of satisfaction" for FBI agents and prosecutors who worked on the investigation and on the legal battle in court.
McVeigh's legacy from the bombing was heightened security against terrorism across America, starting at the White House and extending to wherever there is a federal building.

Just as the 1963 assassination of President John Kennedy meant U.S. political leaders could no longer be considered safe in public, the Oklahoma attack brought home to many Americans the threat that the truck parked close to a building or an abandoned bag left in an airport might contain a bomb.

One significant change was the closing of Pennsylvania Avenue outside the White House, a beloved American thoroughfare that the Secret Service now deems too dangerous to keep open to public motor traffic.

Clinton has ignored appeals to reopen the avenue, convinced by evidence presented by government technical experts that an Oklahoma-like bomb detonated on the street would level the White House and kill many.

The fear of a bomb is such that, when Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O'Connor arrived home on Friday with her usual security contingent to find a box wrapped in black plastic at her front door, five different police organisations responded, fearful it was a bomb.
It turned out to be a pair of shoes she had ordered.
